question.:question/problem:
![](images/ef/efe35f51fa4ce8707e2ac4ce1785ece55e9191bcedbe2b22ff64b5e4510eb5c7.png)

Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line above?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's pick two distinct points on the line. For example, $A$ and $B$ with coordinates $(0,-2)$ and $(2,-1)$, respectively.

![](images/ac/ace116847d9b31abeb947a1e3952dc9f6aea7224602d394d9318efc51476bc6e.png)

Now, we substitute the coordinates of both points in our equations. If both points satisfy an equation, then we can conclude that the equation represents the line in the graph. Otherwise, if any point does *not* satisfy the equation, then we can conclude that the equation does *not* represent the line in the graph.

- Equation: $y=\frac{1}{2}x-2.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-2)$ and $B(2,-1)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2) &=\frac{1}{2}(0)-2 \\ -2 &=-2\,\checkmark \\ (-1) &=\frac{1}{2}(2)-2 \\ -1 &=-1\,\checkmark\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=\frac{1}{2}x-2$ is an equation of the line in the graph.

- Equation: $y=-2+\frac{1}{2}x.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-2)$ and $B(2,-1)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2) &=-2+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\ -2 &=-2\,\checkmark \\ (-1) &=-2+\frac{1}{2}(2) \\ -1 &=-1\,\checkmark\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=-2+\frac{1}{2}x$ is an equation of the line in the graph.

- Equation: $y-2x=-2.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-2)$ and $B(2,-1)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)-2(0) &=-2 \\ -2 &=-2\,\checkmark \\ (-1)-2(2) &=-2 \\ -5 &=-2\,\times\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y-2x=-2$ is *not* an equation of the line in the graph.

Select $y=\frac{1}{2}x-2$, $y=-2+\frac{1}{2}x$.

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $det(M)$, if
 $$
\displaystyle M=\begin{bmatrix}2x & \sqrt{y} \\ \sqrt{y} & -x\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}2x & \sqrt{y} \\ \sqrt{y} & -x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2x\cdot (-x)-\sqrt{y}\cdot \sqrt{y} \\  & =-2{x}^{2}-y\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{7}$ and ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=7$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{7+1}}{7+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{8}}{8}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{x}^{8}}{8}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{1}{8}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8})+0 \\ &= \frac{1}{8}\cdot 8\,{x}^{7} \\ &= {x}^{7}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If
$$
\displaystyle B=\begin{bmatrix}2 & x \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}
$$
and
$\text{det}(B)=2$, what is the value of $x?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(B) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & x \\ 2 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 6-x\cdot 2 \\  & =12-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(B)=2$, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =2 \\ 12-2x & =2 \\ -2x & =2-12 \\ -2x & =-10 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}3+t & 4t \\ -3 & 3-t\end{bmatrix}
$$
and $det(A)=45,$ what is the value of $t?$

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}3+t & 4t \\ -3 & 3-t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(3+t)(3-t)-4t(-3) \\  & =9-{t}^{2}+12t \\  & =-{t}^{2}+12t+9.\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{7/2}}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{7/2}}={x}^{-7/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{7}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-7/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-7/2+1}}{(-\frac{7}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-5/2}}{\left(-\frac{5}{2}\right)}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-5/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{5{x}^{5/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=\frac{33 t^{2}}{2} - 11 t,\qquad y=6 - 6 t^{2}
$$

$$
-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=3$. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t)=33 t - 11,\qquad y'(t)=- 12 t
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{- 12 t}{33 t - 11}=- \frac{12 t}{33 t - 11}
$$

At the point where $t=3$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx}\big|_{t=3}&=\frac{- 12 \left(3\right)}{33 \left(3\right) - 11}\\&=\frac{-36}{88}\\&=- \frac{9}{22}\end{aligned}
$$
